utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom, and to those listening to our procedures. Especially welcome to you, Mr. Sladojevic. I will address the parties about your presence here in a moment. But first I have to raise a serious scheduling problem the Chamber is facing. It turned out that next week on Monday and Tuesday, we are not able to sit, because only one Judge is present. Two Judges are committed to have some other commitments so that it is not possible to sit on Monday and Tuesday of next week. Instead of that, we would like to have a hearing on Friday, the 1st of July -- no, yes, 1st of July, and, in addition, we would like to move our hearing on Wednesday, the 29th of June, to the afternoon. At the moment, if I'm not mistaken, we are scheduled to sit in the morning. We should try to move it to the afternoon. So, in effect, we would have three hearings next week. In the following week, so as not to lose a single court day, we would like to sit, in addition to the four days we are sitting usually, also, on the Friday, the 8th of July. It will be reflected in the court calendar as soon as possible. I hope the parties are able to manage everything, although I suppose it is quite difficult for the Prosecution because of a specific witness who will be one of the next witnesses. Are there any other procedural, or other matters to raise in court today before we start with the next witness? Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, and everyone. The only issue with relation to the next witness I understand you intend to address the parties concerning the Court's position and concerning Mr. Sladojevic's presence here today. And in terms of the proposed scheduling of the Chamber, I can't respond to our position in terms of our ability to facilitate that schedule at the moment. What I would propose to do, however, is to consult with my colleagues over the break, perhaps, and I can come back to you with some useful information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: My apologies with Mr. Vanderpuye. We had problems with our screens. We couldn't follow. But now I think every problem is solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Would like me to repeat my --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. It is in the record, and most of it I catched -- I caught. I was able to follow. After consultation of your colleagues, you may come back to the Court, of course, and there may be some informal exchange of views. That is no problem. But we wanted to let you know as soon as possible. Thank you very much. The next witness should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are turning into closed session for a moment to enable the witness to come into the courtroom. He should be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I neglected to advise the Trial Chamber that I would be asking for a caution, pursuant to Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: First of all, sir, welcome to the courtroom. Good afternoon. Would you please read aloud the affirmation and the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And please sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to address you with some matters. The first is there are still, like in the last trial, some protective measures in place for you. In this case, face distortion. Nobody will recognise you in the public gallery or in the Internet. The second matter I would like to mention is the presence of Mr. Sladojevic. And I would like to give you some kind of guidance, sir. Mr. Savcic, yesterday, one of Mr. Karadzic's legal associates, Marko Sladojevic, informed the Chamber of your function as an investigator in the Karadzic case. The Chamber welcomes you to the courtroom, but before your testimony, the Chamber would like to stress that you appearance here today is in the capacity of a Prosecution witness in the Tolimir case. As such, you will be questioned by the Prosecution and later by the Defence about your knowledge of the events at the time relevant to the indictment against Mr. Tolimir. This concerns your contemporaneous knowledge of the events on the ground in 1995. It does not concern the knowledge you have gained as an investigator for the Defence of Mr. Karadzic. The Chamber expects that you can make this distinction easily. As you will have noted, we have decided to allow Mr. Sladojevic to be present in the courtroom. The Chamber wants to be absolutely clear that this is out of courtesy only. Mr. Sladojevic has no standing before this Chamber. He may not address the Chamber, nor may he address you or interrupt you in the course of your testimony. Should you, in the course of your testimony, feel the need to consult Mr. Sladojevic about areas of evidence concerning which you have gained knowledge as a result of your role as investigator in the other case, and the limitations this may put you under as a result of your work for the Karadzic Defence, you may, upon a request, being granted by the Chamber, consult Mr. Sladojevic, at which time the Chamber will temporarily adjourn the proceedings. I hope this is clear for everybody, and I would like to stress that yesterday we contacted both parties and there were no objection to the requested presence of Mr. Sladojevic, nor by the -- not by the OTP, nor by the Defence. I hope you understood this guidance you just have received.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood it fully, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. On the request of the Prosecution, I would like to give you a caution. In our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, we have the Rule 90 (E) which I would like to read out to you. I quote: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent Prosecution against the witness for any offence, other than false testimony." I hope you understood this term, this rule, as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now it's the turn of Mr. Vanderpuye to commence his examination-in-chief and to put questions to you. Mr. Vanderpuye, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon to you, again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, General Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: You've been here before, but just let me remind you to try and speak a little bit more slowly than you would normally which would give the interpreters to understand and interpret to everyone in the courtroom what you say so that it is clearly understood. And if there's anything that I ask you that is unclear or I ask it in an unclear way, please let me know so that I can try to rephrase it so that we can better understand one another. Let me first ask you the following: Do you recall having testified in the case of Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al between the 11th and 13th of September 2007?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Have you had an opportunity to review your testimony in that case before coming here today?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I had an opportunity to listen to my own testimony before I arrived in the courtroom today.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And, General, having listened to your testimony, do you stand by what you testified to in that case?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. There are a couple of things that I should add and clarify. I don't think that during the last trial I made myself completely clear on a couple of matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this: If you were to be asked the same questions as you were asked in the other case, would your answers, in substance, be the same as they were, aside from the clarifications that you wanted to make?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: In substance, I can't say that my answers would be identical. It is impossible. However, in principle, my answers would be the same as those I gave four years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would offer, at the time, General Savcic's prior testimony, which is 65 ter 7427 under seal and 7428.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Both will be received. The former under seal. One moment, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 7427 shall be assigned Exhibit P2417, admitted under seal. And the 65 ter document 7428 shall be assigned Exhibit P2418. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would also at this time, Mr. President, tender the associated exhibits that were admitted through the witness during the course of his testimony. That is 65 ter 0 -- well, 65 ter 8, 35, 1994, 7092, 7429, and 7433.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. They all will be received as exhibits. 65 ter 7429, under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, 65 ter document 8 shall be assigned Exhibit P2419. 65 ter document 35 shall be assigned Exhibit P2420. 65 ter document 1994 shall be assigned Exhibit P2421. 65 ter document 7092 shall be assigned Exhibit P2422. 65 ter document 7429 shall be assigned Exhibit P2423.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Under seal.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Admitted under seal. And 65 ter document 7433 shall be assigned Exhibit P2424. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I do have a summary of the General's testimony that I'd like to read into the record. It is on the long side of short but I think it would be helpful to the Trial Chamber. General Savcic was born in Sokolac, Bosnia and Herzegovina, in 1959. Throughout his career, he was a professional military officer and completed both the Military Academy in Belgrade and the General Staff school. Between 1992 and 1995, General Savcic was promoted three times, attaining the rank of colonel in 1995. On 30th July 2002, he retired from active service with the rank of lieutenant-general. In early June 1992, then-Captain First Class Savcic joined the VRS. He was assigned as a chief -- as the Chief of Staff of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. He performed this function and that of acting commander of the unit until his formal appointment as commander in September 1992. The regiment's deputy commander was Lieutenant-Colonel Jovo Jazic. During Commander Savcic's hospitalisation for a combat injury between 12 October 1994 and 23 June 1995, Jazic commanded the regiment. The main tasks of the 65th Protection Regiment were providing security for the Main Staff command posts, ensuring safe work conditions for the organ of the Main Staff command -- organs of the Main Staff command and securing high-level officers and carrying out other orders of the superior command. In 1995, the regiment's command included assistant commanders for morale, religious and legal affairs, and for logistics, in addition to Savcic and Jazic. The establishment post of an assistant commander for intelligence and security was not filled. The regiment was comprised of a number of specialised units and could be deployed in offensive and defensive combat actions. The units included a sabotage unit, tank, logistics, transport, and mortar companies as well as motorised artillery rocket anti-aircraft defence and military police battalions. The military police battalion consisted of four companies and was mainly responsible for securing command posts, military leaders, documents, assets and equipment. In July 1995, parts of the 1st and 2nd companies were engaged in combat in Treskavica, some distance from Sarajevo, and Trnovo in the area of responsibility of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. At that time 3rd and 4th Companies primarily secured the command posts in the at Crna Rijeka. As of 1993, the military police battalion command was located in Nova Kasaba. Major Zoran Malinic was the MP commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down a bit. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: He received his orders from the regiment commander, who, in turn, directly -- was directly subordinated to General Mladic. Captain Aleksandar Lucic was the MP battalion's deputy commander. Following General Savcic's return to the regiment command post on the 23rd of June, 1995, he was briefed on the state of the regiment and in the BiH, and Generals Mladic and Tolimir visited him. General Mladic tasked him with reassessing the security of the Main Staff command post, which he set about doing. Shortly thereafter, on the 26th of June, the command post was attacked. Having secured the Main Staff command, General Savcic was given a new task: To engage in reconnaissance actions toward Zepa. He carried out these activities in the Borike and Rogatica sectors until 14 July 1995, when he was assigned to carry out an attack against the ABiH, Zepa Brigade in the Gusinac sector. During the period that Savcic remained in Borike, more precisely in the sector of Sjeversko village, General Tolimir was also present at this location. Although General Savcic could not recall when General Tolimir arrived, he testified that General Tolimir was present there on 13 July 1995. On the morning of 13 July 1995, Savcic received a radio call from Major Malinic who was in Nova Kasaba. Malinic reported having received two or three prisoners. When General Savcic spoke again with Major Malinic later that morning, Malinic advised that the situation was becoming more complex and that a continuous stream of men from Srebrenica were surrendering. Major Malinic said that there were many prisoners and that he was completely helpless to secure them with the forces he had in Nova Kasaba. General Savcic testified that he told Malinic to request from Lieutenant-Colonel Jazic then at the regiment command in Crna Rijeka, the assistance of the armoured units deployed to Crna Rijeka. General Tolimir knew about the situation developing in Nova Kasaba. According to Savcic, "He was around, standing next to me" during the conversation with Malinic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I interrupt you for a moment. Mr. Tolimir wants to raise something. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I greet everyone present and I hope this court day will end in keeping with God's will, and I welcome General Savcic. Wish him a nice day among us. I would appreciate it if Mr. Vanderpuye would quote what the witness said without making assertions regarding General Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is up to the Prosecutor to present the summary of previous testimony as he wishes to put it to the Chamber. But I would like to repeat, it is not evidence. It is just to inform the Chamber and the public about previous testimony and the way he understands the previous testimony. It is not evidence. Please carry on, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. For the record, the last section that I just read was a quote, and it's from the transcript page of a prior proceedings 15256, lines 6 through 13. General Savcic further testified about a 13 July document from the 65th Protection Regiment IKM in Borike - in this case it is P125 - in which General Tolimir proposed procedures for the treatment of the 1.000-plus prisoners in Nova Kasaba. General Savcic noted that the document did not bear his handwritten signature but bore his type written name, although it was not in the format of a telegram. He also observed that it lacked a stamp as well as a date. Nevertheless, he testified that he "cannot refute the possibility with 100 per cent certainty" that he, in fact, drafted a document, as dictated by General Tolimir. He opined that if the document had been transmitted, this would have been done from the Rogatica Brigade. As concerns the substance of the document, General Savcic was asked what, if any, military reason there would be -- there was, I'm sorry, for the proposal to replace prisoners indoors or in an area protected from observation from the ground or the air as set out in item 3 in the document. Acknowledging his indefinite answer to the question, to this same question during his 2005 OTP interview, General Savcic offered the following explanation: First, that such a proposal could have been made because NATO aircraft who controlled the air-space at the time, might mistake the prisoners assembled on the football pitch for Serb soldiers and fire on them. Second, another possible explanation for the proposal could be that it would be more difficult to guard the prisoners in an open area at night. Finally, General Savcic assumed that the assistant commander for security and intelligence must have had in mind the Geneva Conventions which, according to the witness, provide that prisoners should not be exposed to the general public. He could offer no further explanation. General Savcic admitted speaking to Major Malinic about this document P125, following his September 2005 OTP interview. Although he claimed that he did not discuss any specifics about the document with Major Malinic, he testified that Malinic told him that he neither received nor was aware of the document. General Savcic testified about the tasks and responsibilities of the VRS Main Staff security organs. He noted, inter alia, that the administration had a military police department which dealt with professional matters of military policing and was responsible for drafting plans and programmes, combat training and equipment for MP units. Colonel Beara was the chief of the security administration, and immediately subordinate to General Tolimir. As such, General Tolimir "was the one to inform about the duties he (Beara) had carried out and to receive new tasks." General Savcic further testified about the principles of subordination regarding the deployment of MUP units in combat, stating that in such situations MUP special brigade units were -- are resubordinated to the military unit in whose area of responsibility combat operations take place. From 15 to 25 July 1995, General Savcic was engaged in combat activities towards Zepa. He was tasked with neutralising ABiH forces in the Gusinac sector and capturing the area of Brezova Ravan. His units achieved this objective on or about the 25th of July, 1995, which in essence ended the military defence of Zepa. Thereafter, the units of the 65th Protection Regiment did not enter Zepa, although General Savcic went to the UNPROFOR check-point briefly. Upon his return to Brezova Ravan, he received an order to return to Han Pijesak and deploy his units to the barracks there in reserve. This concludes my summary, Mr. President, and I do have some questions for General Savcic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: General, it's been a number of years since you were last here, and we've heard that you are an investigator now with the Karadzic Defence. Let me just ask you: How long have you been engaged as an investigator by the Karadzic Defence?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Since 2009. I believe the decision of the Registry appointing me an investigator on that Defence team dates back to July 2009. So it will a two full years soon.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As you may know, this case involves the events that transpired in the areas of Srebrenica and Zepa in 1995. Has your work as a Defence investigator put you in contact with witnesses that are relevant to that period of time and the circumstances of this case, as you understand it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Do you mean witnesses concerning Srebrenica and Zepa?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know how well acquainted those present in the courtroom are with the dynamics of the trial of Mr. Karadzic, but at the current stage, the Prosecution is leading evidence on Sarajevo, and we have, so far, also been dealing mainly with that matter. Since, according to the Prosecution's schedule, Srebrenica comes at the end of their case, we have also planned our time and resources for that issue for some time in the future. But, of course, if, in the course of our current work we come across something relevant, we don't disregard it but, so far, we haven't had any contact with such witnesses. We have made a preliminary list of our witnesses, and we haven't contacted Prosecution witnesses at all. We fully observe the rules regarding contacts with witnesses and if we want to contact a witness, we make a request through the Registry. They contact the witness, and then the witness decided whether or not to agree to talk to the Defence. That's the rule. We don't do anything outside of the rules. I hope that's an answer to your question, if I understood it in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: It is. Thank you very much. Have you been in contact with your subordinates; for example, in the 65th Protection Regiment, Motorised Protection Regiment, in the context of your investigative work for the Karadzic Defence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm not sure if this is a good line of question --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- in relation to his position as a member of the Defence team in the Karadzic case. Of course, it is up to the witness to decide and to make a distinction between those matters relevant to this case here or his duty as a Defence investigator in the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I raise the issue only because first I'm not asking as to the substance of the contact, but, clearly, any contact between this witness and his subordinates in the regiment to the extent that it may relate to or affect the substance of those subordinates' evidence in this trial, I think is relevant. But, obviously if it's a question of the substance and deals with confidences or privileges, then that is another matter. But I'm not asking for those. I'm just asking whether or not he has had contact with them in his capacity as an investigator, at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But there may be a problem for the witness, even the fact of a contact to a witness itself may be one -- part of the area of confidential information in the other case. Not only the content of -- possible contact to a witness, or from a subordinate, if it was -- if this witness was contacted by the Investigator Savcic in his capacity as an investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I understand that. I just -- I don't see that it is covered under Rule 97 which relates to privileges and confidences between attorneys and clients as an investigator. But I do respect that, and I understand the Court's position. So I'm trying to steer clear of that to make matters, I think, more expeditious and simple, but I don't think I've quite transgressed on that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: As of yet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just want to make it clear that it is exactly the difficulty in this -- during this testimony of the witness to make this distinction between his two roles he has to play. On the other hand, it is up to the witness to decide if he is able to answer such a question or not. Or if the true and truthful answer would violate his obligations as a member of the Defence team. It is not up to this Chamber to decide on that. But please be aware of the difficulty which such a question could create for the witness. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Are you able to answer the question, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I can. Once a year in the third week of August, approximately, members of the 65th Protection Regiment gather to share memories, to socialise a bit to see who is still alive, who is in what state of health, but I have not contacted a single member of the 65th Protection Regiment in my capacity as investigator. With each potential witness and each source of information, or potential source of information, I do exactly what Mr. Karadzic has asked. I advise them at the outset that everyone should tell only the truth and only their direct knowledge about matters of interest to us. So I'm not considering, actually, any members of the 65th Regiment as potential witnesses because I can't imagine what they could possibly tell that would be of interest in this case or the Karadzic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Just remind us, you retired in 2002; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. And I believe, looking at the record on the LiveNote, that there's a mistake. You said I was retired as lieutenant-general, which is not correct. I was -- I was retired as a major-general.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is not quite certain. We will check.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe that you said that you were retired as a general, "potpukovnik." Is that what you said, "potpukovnik"?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: General, "potpukovnik" is actually lieutenant-general. The witness earlier said that Mr. Vanderpuye had said he had retired as colonel-general and that is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, what the record should reflect is "lieutenant-general," which is how it is translated in the -- in the transcript of your prior testimony. But, in any event, thank you for that clarification. What position other than your rank, what position did you retire from?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I don't think I understand that question. You mean what position I occupied last before I retired?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Well, practically, I had no position or responsibility. I was on stand by at the General Staff of the VRS, and the reason for that was my state of health at the time, which was certified by the competent military medical panel. I was unfit for service.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Before you became unfit for service, what position did you hold in the VRS, after the events of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Well, I became unfit for professional military service back in 1994, on the 12th of October, due to the serious wounds I sustained. But after a while, I just continued to serve through a sheer exercise of will, because I was still young. And in 1995, for a while, for about a year or so, perhaps 15 months, I was chief of the security administration in the VRS.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to show you P104. And I'd like to go to -- it's a map. And I'd like to show you map number 10 in this exhibit. It may be a little bit difficult to see on that monitor where you are. We've had some trouble with that in the past. So if you are unable to see the image clearly, please let us know and we can try to adjust it so that you can. Or you can, if you're able, stand a little bit and maybe halfway and you can see it more clearly. I'd like to just focus in, if we can, a little more. If we can blow it up some, on the area from Han Pijesak -- yeah that's fine. Okay. Maybe we can -- Can you see this clearly, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I see for the most part. Yes, I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There's a couple of questions I wanted to ask you about this. Here we can see certain locations that are marked in English. VRS headquarters. And then, to the right of that, we see Krivace IKM and then Podzeplje IKM. Immediately beneath the VRS headquarters, we can see something here that's written 65th Protection Regiment base. And then to the left of that, we can see the Jela restaurant. In terms of the 65th Projection base, can you confirm that it was at the location that is indicated at this -- on this exhibit, and what base that is? What units were at this base.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I don't know who gave you this map. There are thousands of IKMs here, forward command posts, which is absolutely untrue. What is correct here is location of the command post of the VRS. You see, it is south-east to this location, Veliki Zep, 1537 metres altitude, and everything else is lower than Veliki Zep. Krivace IKM, forward command post, did not exist, as far as the Protection Regiment is concerned. I don't know if anybody had a command post there. Podzeplje forward command post, a permanent unit, the size of a squad or two squads, that means 10 to 15 men, was constantly at Krivace but not at this location of the regiment but in the broader area.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would like for you to focus just on the area, for the moment, that is marked 65th Protection Regiment, and maybe we can blow it up so that we can see just VRS headquarters and 65th Protection Regiment for the moment. And maybe we will be able to see Veliki Zep and some of these features that the witness has been talking about. Okay. Are you able now to see the area that I'd like you to focus on, which is the circle that's marked 65th Protection Regiment base? And if you can't, let us know, because we can just the screen so that you can see it. You see immediately above that Veliki Zep?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that well. However, that location did not exist. There were no members of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment. This road that goes around Veliki Zep, beginning with Han Pijesak to the south of Veliki Zep and comes back to Crna Rijeka and goes back. That is a ring around Veliki Zep. The location of the regiment where it says VRS HQ, the deployment of the regiment is to the north of the VRS HQ, 300 or 400 metres away. The units were deployed first in the woods, then under tents. And only sometime in 1995 did we start building some hutments above ground, whereas we had been in dugouts previously. Because this is a mountainous area. The winters are long and very harsh. Where it says Han Pijesak, not in Han Pijesak but approximately under the letter K, it was 300, 400 metres from this circle marking the location of the VRS HQ. Now, this base of the regiment at the cross-roads -- sorry. I'm wrong again. That's the command post of the motorised battalion that belonged to the regiment. I believe it was under Plana. This circle where it says regiment base, that was the command post of the motorised battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That was the command post of the motorised battalion. Yes, because I'm not asking you specifically about the headquarters for the command post of the regiment, as it were. But of this particular location, this was the base of a -- of a motorised battalion. Is that essentially what you said?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I was trying to be very precise. At that spot, there was only the command of the motorised battalion that was stationed. The command is a part of the battalion that commands the battalion, and together with the logistical elements, catering to 10 to 15 men; whereas, the battalion was engaged and active in different locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So let me just confirm that what we have marked here as the 65th Protection Regiment base was the command of a motorised battalion of the 65th Protection Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Excellent.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Which battalion was located -- which battalion command was located there?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: The one and only motorised battalion that was on the strength of the Protection Regiment. There was just one motorised battalion. The rest were different types of battalions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: We can zoom out a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And I want to take -- I would like to take you to a different location at the -- well, let me just confirm one thing before we move on. The location of the battalion command, was that in Podplane [phoen]?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Correct, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let's go to the south part of this map. Not too south. And I would like to focus the witness, if I could, from Boksanica to Borike villa and blow that up. I think this will do. And you will let us know if not. You see an area which can indicated as Borike IKM. Can you see that, General?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The area that's indicated Borike IKM, is that an area where you were during some period of time in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I was south of that where it says Borike villa. It is a facility where I stayed only during the night when I had some time to rest. That facility was commissioned by the prime minister of the former republic, Dzemal Bijedic. It is still in a good state of repair. It consists of several rooms where you can spend the night. I stayed there only when I had time to rest. But I didn't stay in just one place when I was in Borike. From Borike, I carried out reconnaissance activities in the direction of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So you can confirm that you stayed in Borike villa, which is south of Borike IKM, as indicated on this map. What facility was at Borike IKM? And did you go there - not stay there - but did you go there during any period in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you that with any absolute certainty. I would like the Trial Chamber to understand one thing. During that period of time, from the 26th of June, when I was attacked, or, rather, when the command post of the Main Staff was attacked, and it happens very rarely in the history of warfare that a facility like that comes under attack. I could tell you a very interesting story about all of the facilities and the attack that ensued from 1992 to 1995. If there's an opportunity to do that, maybe you will want to hear that story. I had about 30 soldiers there. I didn't have anybody else, no assistants of mine were there. Therefore, there was no need for me to develop an IKM. It was impossible because such a facility would imply space, resource, people. I didn't have any of that. I was in command of an assault group that started as a reconnaissance group and then became an assault group. I had direct command over them. I did not have any elements that would help me to develop an IKM. I would have had to have at least two or three of my assistants, I would have had to have some communications tools, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: My question is very simply, did you go there or not? And, alternatively -- well, not alternatively, but if you know what was there? That's all. I don't need to know if you had people there to see or not to see. I just want to know, for the moment, if you went there in July of 1995. Not June or August, but in July.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, with all due respect, I absolutely don't understand what do you mean when you say "did you go there"? You are asking me, did you go there? What's there?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: To the area, or the facility that's marked on the map as Borike IKM. Did you go there? If you don't remember, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: When it comes to the Protection Regiment, an IKM did not exist. The only facility in Borike was the villa facility where we spent a night -- where we spent a night or two. I don't know how many nights. I don't know of any other facility that you refer to. As far as I know, no such facility ever existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Let me show you P125. Now, I'm going to come back to this document in a little while, and I don't want to dwell on it right now. And I know you've seen this document before on a number of occasions. So let me just cut right to the chase and ask you, at the very top of the screen on the left-hand side, you can see what's clearly marked here - if we can blow that up, thank you - IKM 65 ZMTP. Can you tell us what 65 ZMTP is? Just that question.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: The 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. As a rule, the names of the units should be in miniscule letters. I repeat, there was no command post in Borike. I did not develop any because I did not have manpower, I did not have the necessary resources.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Next to what is written here we can see very clearly, IKM; correct? Next to 65th ZMTP we see, to the left of it, IKM; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I absolutely do not contest what is says here. But I do contest the things as you portray them because that's not how they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm not asking if you contest it. I'm asking you, do you see what is clearly marked here as IKM next to 65 ZMTP? This is a simple question, yes or no. You see it or you don't.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I've already told you loud and clear, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you see beneath that it's written Borike at 1400 hours; right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we can zoom out a moment. And we can go to the bottom right of the corner -- bottom right of the document, we can see what's printed here as komandant pukovnik, Milomir Savcic. P. Pukovnik, Milomir Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Right. This is typed up, Commander Lieutenant-Colonel Milomir Savcic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I'll come back to this document in a moment. And if we can go back to map number 10, at P104, I'd like to ask you some questions about the villa, the Borike villa. If we can zoom back in on the area that we had before. You mentioned that you stayed at Borike villa for some period of time in July 1995; is that right? On and off?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I would not call that staying there. That sounds like a tourist holiday. I spent a couple of nights there.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And where is that located, if you can remember? Specifically, what town?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Well, that is in the Borike village sector. As far as I can remember -- or, rather, according to what I know, it was a farm that also had a farm of Bosnian horses, working horses, as well as riding horses. In the area of that farm, or an agriculture combine -- I don't know what to call it. In any case, they were a farming company, and the villa was there within that perimeter and there was a hotel as well, and there was also the village of Borike with an Orthodox church in the centre of the village. So that would be all that I can tell you about the location. All of the facilities that I've just mentioned are located in the territory of Rogatica municipality, but they are some 40 or so kilometres away from Rogatica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was that in Sjeversko village?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: We have not mentioned Sjeversko yet, have we? Sjeversko is a village that, as far as I can remember, is north of Borike or maybe north-east of Borike; I'm not sure. Many years have passed since. I remember that they used to have a school there, but that school was closed down, because there was not enough children. In any case, the entire area, just to help you understand things -- the entire area is known as the Borike sector. There a lot of hamlets and villages there that I have forgotten in the meantime.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's fine. Let me move to a different area. You testified in the Popovic case that you did not have an assistant commander for security intelligence within the regiment. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember it, and also I have just listened to the audio recording of my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And so, in terms of handling these matters that were within the sphere of competence of the security and intelligence sector, say, within the regiment, was that done through or by the organs of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I already stated last time that, in principle, when a unit is -- does not have a security organ, counter-intelligence tasks are performed by some other security organ according to the principles of security. Since we were a unit of the Main Staff, it was only logical that somebody from the security department did that. Maybe it's the security administration. I can't even use proper terms anymore. It was a long time ago. So if I sometimes misspeak, when I say an administration and I mean a department, please don't hold it against me. The -- the whole service became an administration later when I was chief. But that's all they do. Counter-intelligence, that falls within the purview of the normal work of a security organ, if such an organ does not exist in a unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me show you 65 ter 3986. Sir, this is a document that is dated 2nd of March, 1995. And that would have been during the period of time that you were in hospital, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And it's a document that shows certain information that's received from the MUP concerning a Muslim fugitive, as you can see here, as is indicated, from Zepa. And the information is relayed to the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. You can see that designation as one of the recipients of the document. If we go right to the first paragraph you can see here that it -- the Main Staff, from whom it is sent, intelligence and security sector says: "From the RS MUP state security department we received a telegram containing intelligence information ... from a fugitive from Zepa." And then it says: "Compare the results of the interview done by the MUP with your information." If we look at the substance of the document we can see here it talks about this interview that was conducted and information obtained, in the second paragraph, about the so-called BiH army, in particular, the 8th Operations Group, Light Viteska Zepa Brigade. And then if we go down to the third paragraph, we will see the extent of the detail that is relayed to your unit about this interview. And it talks about the Zepa Brigade, Light Viteska Brigade, I should say, that it has, 1220 conscripts. It talks about the brigade staff commanded by Avdo Palic and deputy commander of Dzevad Brgulja. We'll go to the next page. We'll see that it talks about the headquarters location in the second paragraph. And it talks about the presence of municipal authorities, also in the following paragraph, such as the president of the municipality of Zepa being located in the same headquarters. If we go to the following page in English, we can see it talks about the composition of the brigade, the companies that make it up. You can see, I think, here, yes, you can see it in the B/C/S. Talks about the 2nd Company, 3rd Company, 4th, and so on, all the way through the logistics company. And if we go to the sixth page of this document in the B/C/S -- I mean, in the English, I think we'll find this on the fourth page in the B/C/S, it talks about when the last inspection of the company was carried out. It talks about Naser Oric meeting with Avdo Palic. You can see that at the bottom of the page in the English. I see it's the third from the last paragraph in the B/C/S. And if we go to the last page of this document, we can see the name of General-major Zdravko Tolimir. We can see a signature. And the second-to-last paragraph we can see that it talks about the poor living conditions and shortages the population of Zepa is experiencing. And he says that this strives towards leaving the enclave. So the first thing I want to ask about this document in particular is, the kind of information that you see here, was this the kind of information that was conveyed to you by the security and intelligence administration of the Main Staff in dealing with these matters for your unit, since your unit didn't have, so to speak, an independent security or intelligence organ?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: It seems to me that here somebody signed on behalf of General Tolimir, if I'm not mistaken. The document was signed on behalf of General Tolimir. This is just a remark in passing because there's no dispute about this document. Yes, it is the task of a security organ to provide army units -- let me tell you that this is a strategic organ who should have the most intelligence that he collects from subordinated units and then in co-operation with the sector of state security. His main task, the task of the security organ, is to gather intelligence about the enemy and provide subordinated units with timely information about the enemy, the deployment of its troops, its intentions, and so on and so forth. So that is the main daily task of a security organ, to assess the enemy. And, based on that, distribute intelligence to the subordinated units, to the extent needed by that particular unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. Did you receive this kind of information regularly from the security and intelligence administration? Your unit, that is.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Regularly concerning intelligence about the enemy that we were engaged with, that was primarily the Zepa Brigade, the forces of the 28th Division. I did not need intelligence about the 5th Corps from Bihac or the 4th from Mostar. I received intelligence about the enemy that threatened me, about what was going on in -- around me. It is very relative when you say regular. The intelligence had to be topical. Regularity is not an issue, because things did not have to happen every seven days or a fortnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender 3986, 65 ter 3986.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 3986 shall be assigned Exhibit P2425. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 4021.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, let me just ask you: During your prior testimony, you also testified about what you referred to as the pursuit and search duty of the military police. Do you remember that? It was at page 15232 and 15233 of your prior testimony.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. I remember that. However, I think that this may be a good occasion to repeat what I said at the beginning. And that is that I should supplement some of the things from my previous testimony. If you agree, it won't take much time, and let me tell you what those things are. Quite inadvertently, I neglected the fact that went it comes to the military police that the military police did not execute only military policing tasks. You will remember that we have a spoken about the structure of the Protection Regiment and I told you that at the beginning, the structure was envisaged as a single unit with a dominant role played by security intelligence organs. It doesn't really matter when that structure was drafted. It was drafted before the war at the level of the former state. However, you have to bear in mind that military police units order the rules governing the work of the military police envisaged that they have to perform security tasks for the military [as interpreted]. Unfortunately, in the last war, that was their ancillary task and their main task, the main task of the military police was to carry out combat activities. Commanders in situations when they didn't have any reserves, when they didn't have enough troops, more often than not, they would reach for military police units and that applied to all levels, from the brigade to the Main Staff. When such a military police unit was engaged in classical combat it did not perform classical military policing tasks. And this is where we had to draw a line between controlling military police units by the security organ in professional terms. I have not seen this before but I am familiar -- I know who the author of the note is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me just ask you a couple of questions about this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should do this after the break, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I should tell you, that at the pace that I'm going, and as you can see I'm trying to be brief, it doesn't seem very likely that I'm going to be able to conclude my direct examination in an hour and a half. By my count, I have probably used close to an hour already, and I'm on the second document of a number of documents that I intend to show the witness. I will do my best to tighten it up when we get back. But unfortunately, I was not able to proof this witness, and there are a number of documents he hasn't seen before, which may occasion somewhat lengthy answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that explanation. We must have our first break and will resume quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, before today, we received your estimation that you need one hour and a half. Up to now, you have used one hour and 16 minute, I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But if there is no objection by the other side, you shall use your time and take your time to finish the examination, but try to be as short as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will do my best, Mr. President. I did point out that unfortunately General Savcic declined to be proofed, so there are a number of documents that he hasn't seen that I wanted to show him, and that may occasion somewhat lengthen the answers. I will try to be as direct as I can in my question with him and hopefully we can get through this quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes, I noted before we had our break that you didn't have that possibility -- the opportunity to proof the witness. That was on his request, I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There is one other issue and that is with respect to the Court's proposed scheduling. I have had an opportunity to receive some information from my colleagues, and I understand that we are fine and we will be able to proceed in accordance with the Trial Chamber's schedule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We had 65 ter 4021 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, and I was just going to ask you a few questions about this document, General. First, we can see that it is signed by an individual, by the name of Mitrovic. Looks like Njegos Mitrovic. Do you know who that person is?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: The signature says Petrovic. I don't see clearly, but I know that it is Njegos Petrovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Mitrovic"], not Mitrovic [Realtime transcript read in error "Petrovic"], like all the men called Njegos.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Was he a member of -- well, how do you know him?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I know him as a professional serviceman in the rank of staff-sergeant, who was commander of the section for military police service.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could that part of the document in B/C/S be enlarged, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Commander --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. On page 34, line 6, it says that's Njegos Mitrovic, not Petrovic. I'm not quite sure that the witness said that. I would just like Mr. Vanderpuye to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think the witness said the opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The witness said the opposite and it was translated the opposite way. It should be Petrovic and not Mitrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you for that, Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Sir, you were saying that he was a member of the military police service. Of what unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: So, in the section of the specials, in the military police battalion. In the military police section that belongings to the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: The military police battalion of what unit? Of your unit? Of a different corps unit? Which unit?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: The military police battalion of the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. Here we can see that it's compiled on the premises of the military police battalion. And it concerns joint military and police task carried out in the Skelani sector, pursuant to a Main Staff order. And it says from what appears to be 16 May 1995. It refers to in the second paragraph that on -- well, it says on 17th May, 1995, following this strictly confidential order 01-1-9, issued by General Mladic and an oral order given by General Tolimir, that a military police platoon was dispatched to Skelani. And at the end of that paragraph it says that their task was to bring deserters in and to seize misappropriated weapons and military equipment. The first thing I want to know is, to what extent are you aware or were you aware of this particular order and the circumstances that it refers to in 1995? To your recollection?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, you see, you said the date was the 16th May 1995. At that time, I was still being treated. So I didn't know about this order, but the order is perfectly regular. And according to this order, members of the military police, through the requesting service of the military police, are searching for persons responsible for disciplinary violations going absent without official leave or other offences, so there's nothing disputable about this, but I did not know about this order, because I was still being treated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 4021 shall be assigned Exhibit P2426. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you 65 ter 7367, please. This is a document, Mr. President, that was not part of the Prosecution's original 65 ter list. It relates, however, to the substance of the witness's prior testimony. In particular, with respect to the role of the military police and the 65th Protection Regiment, as concerns misconduct by officers, or, rather, by -- by soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, can you help me? I don't see it in the list of -- yes, I see it. Sorry. Yes. Mr. Tolimir, my usual question: Do you have any objections to add this document to the 65 ter exhibit list? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the Defence has no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Leave is granted. Mr. Vanderpuye, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: What we have here, General, is a document that is issued by the Main Staff, in particular, the security administration. It's dated 24 August 1995. And comes from naval captain Ljubisa Beara. And you can see in this particular document it is directed to the military police battalion of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment and to the commander personally. First, that would be the commander of the military police battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Who do you mean was commander of the military police?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Maybe it's a translation issue. The document is directed to the military police battalion of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment. And then it says, "To the commander personally." So is that the commander of the regiment or the commander of the battalion? Or some other commander.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Since it's addressed to the battalion of the military police, when it says underneath "to the commander," that means commander of the military police battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And that would have been Zoran Malinic, Major, on 24th August 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: At that time, yes, he was Major Zoran Malinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this document, we see here that there's an investigation going on with respect to the conduct of Lieutenant Miladin Matic. First of all, do you know who Miladin Matic is or was back in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I see you smiling. Are you familiar with this document or the subject matter of it?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Both. But most of all I'm familiar with Miladin Matic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In this document, Colonel Beara indicates that Lieutenant Matic lied when he said that he did not take money from captured prisoners. As you can -- will see in the documentation that accompanies this. And it says that he will give a statement regarding these circumstances which you, meaning the commander of the military police battalion, will send to the security administration for further determination. Now, in this particular case, you can see at the very last paragraph it says: "Please note that it is the explicit order of the commander of the Main Staff, Colonel-General Ratko Mladic, that nothing must be taken from the," it says "redacted," "whom we evacuated from Zepa and that they must not be maltreated." And it's signed by Naval Captain Ljubisa Beara. Just so that we are clear, and I know you've testified about this before, at that point in time, what position did Colonel Beara hold, or Naval Captain Beara hold?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: The chief of the security administration, I'm afraid to be wrong about the terms, but I see that it says "security administration."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, with respect to this particular document, would it have been the normal scope of the security intelligence sector, and, indeed, the security administration, to instruct the commander of the military police battalion of your unit on matters such as what is indicated here; that is, the apparently criminal conduct of Lieutenant Matic with respect to taking property from prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: As far as the substance of the assignment is concerned, it falls within the jurisdiction of the security organs. That is, to provide professional guidance to the military police. So information is provided here that Matic had done something he should not have done. There were no command orders to do that. And it's actually a report. It says the lieutenant is informing about what he had done about it, and that he would provide a statement to the security administration for their further decision-making. But for the Trial Chamber and for you as a Prosecutor, I need to say what kind of person this man was. That's why I smiled a moment ago. Miladin Matic was a NCO before the war. He served in the military police of the 4th Corps, then Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, then Drina Corps, and he seems to have moved from post to post, from unit to unit very fast because he couldn't stand the regiment, et cetera. So I was frankly surprised when, in July, 1995, that he was around -- to see that he was around, and I insisted that he be removed from the military police and that was later done. Because he was a man who caused a lot of problems in general, and before he was in my unit and when he was in my unit, I didn't agree with his methods of work, and I wanted him out. But as for this report from the battalion, this is just information to the administration and the administration will later decide what to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to ask the witness to slow down a little because it's very difficult to follow the translation, and I think the interpreters find it hard to get absolutely everything the witness is saying. To avoid the need to check the transcript again, I would like to ask the witness to slow down a little.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This proposal is appreciated and is also the -- the proposal of the Chamber. Please don't respond too fast. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would just like to go to the next page, if I can, in the B/C/S and also in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here what we see, General, is a document that you can see is signed under the name Vujadin Popovic. Do you, first of all, recognise the name?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: I know Vujadin Popovic. And I know who he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. At that time, he was the chief of security at -- with the Drina Corps; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Here he says that he has attached the statements of military policemen from the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade who were present during the robbing committed by Lieutenant Matic and also returning the 100 Deutschemarks, which the policemen did not spend, of the 170 given to them by Lieutenant Matic. It would be normal for this procedure to have been followed in relation to the actions that Mr. Matic apparently engaged in. Is that -- that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to go just to the next page. In both, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And here we can see another document appended to -- apprehended. Where we have another report by Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic, where he says -- and it's directed to the Main Staff of the VRS, and it says: "Reference, your verbal order for the persons who robbed the Balija to be found." And he indicates here the same thing that we are going to return, or we are returning the 100 Deutschemarks that the policemen did not spend of the 170, and so on and so forth. And again, this would be an appropriate procedure to follow in light of the apparently criminal actions that Mr. Matic had engaged in. Is that fair?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page of both documents, we'll see the attached statements of the military policemen of the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade, who were present and describe the events that Mr. Matic is -- was apparently investigated for. And we will see -- I don't want to go into all of the details here, but we can see that at least in the first paragraph of this statement given by Dragisa Bijelogrlic [phoen], he says that on the 28th, 29th of July, 1995, he was in the Luke sector together with other policemen and members of the engineers platoon of this brigade, the 1st Vlasenica Light Infantry Brigade, for the purpose of inspecting convoys and separating men fit for military service who were trying to go from the direction of Zepa towards Kladanj with civilians. And he says basically that members of the military police were responsible for guarding and registering the men who had been separated. If we go to the next page in the English, he describes that Matic basically shows up at a school where these men are being held and he demands money from the Muslims, and it says: "Matic also said that he had received an order to search the Muslims who had been detained and to take away from them all valuables, especially money." And so on and so forth. And, again, this would be an appropriate procedure to follow with respect to dealing with the actions of Mr. Matic. Is that fair? That is, to attach the statements of the witness to the -- to the activity.

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Correct. To complete the file with the material evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Do I understand it correctly that it is a -- together some documents as concluded in one. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That's correct. It's the attachments to the main document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There are two statements, the witness statements. Then there are two reports from Mr. Popovic, and I believe those are apprehended to the document from Mr. Beara. So five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter 7367 shall be assigned Exhibit P2427. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show you, General, 65 ter 5807. And what we have here, General, is a document which is an order on the preparation and organisation for a briefing on the combat readiness of the VRS for the year 1994, as you may know, which occurred in 1995. The date of document is 23 January 1995. First of all, are you aware, or were you -- I know you were in the hospital during this period of time, but were you aware that such a briefing occurred early in 1995 before your return to the regiment command post?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Well, about specific reporting on combat readiness, I did not know, although it is a planned and regular activity of all units and the army as a whole that is carried out every year.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to briefly take you through some of the substance of this document. As you indicated, it was a -- an annual event. And we can see that it is based on the annual work-plan of the Main Staff of the VRS with -- with respect to carrying out an analysis and assessment of the execution of the tasks in 1994. If we go to the next page, we will see the order itself. In the order it talks about, essentially, the scheduling of this event from the 29th of January through the 31st. And it directs that unit commanders conduct a briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If we go to the following page, I think in both documents, yes, we will see a reference to 30th January 1995. And it refers to an analysis to be conducted in the presence of the highest state and political organs of the RS. And at the very bottom of that section, on the -- in the English, and item (b) in the B/C/S we'll see here that says: "Conclusions from the assessment of the situation on the front and an operational and strategic assessment of the further course of the war with a proposal of measures ..." and that's to be carried out by the chief of the intelligence and security sector. And that would be General Tolimir, wouldn't it, at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes that would have been his duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And under item --

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Or, rather, that would have been the duty of the sector that he headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Very well. And under item 3 (c) for January 31st, 1995, I think it's right at the bottom of the page in the B/C/S and it's on page -- it should be page 5 -- the next page in the English. We see that with respect to the collegium of the commander of the Main Staff, that present at the briefing should be commanders of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment and the 67th Communication Regiment. Do you see that there under item (c)?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. The translation is somewhat awkward. "Communication Regiment."

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you aware of a unit called the 67th Communication Regiment?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Of course, I was aware of it. It was a staff unit, located in Crna Rijeka at the command post. Of course I knew about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: So the commander of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment that would have been or was supposed to have been present at this briefing, who would that have been in your absence, since you were in the hospital, I think, at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: A person who was acting as -- as the commander -- a commander. Actually, the person standing in for the commander, that was the Chief of Staff or his deputy by establishment. And this is an extended collegium. And when a collegium is in session, in this composition, that's without the commander of staff units, and it was common practice for nobody beyond the rank of general to be present at the collegium. But it all depended on the topics that were discussed that were on the agenda of the commander's collegium meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm a little confused by your answer. The document here indicates commanders of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment should be present. So if you, as the commander of the 65th Motorised Protection Regiment were unavailable because you were in the hospital, who would have been there in your place? And I think your answer says the Chief of Staff or his deputy by establishment. But are you referring to the Chief of Staff of the regiment or the Chief of Staff of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: The author of the document is not interested in whether the commander of the Protection Regiment is in hospital. Somebody has to be in command. And that's why he says commander. And if that is not a person by establishment, then it's his deputy, the Chief of Staff or the deputy commander of the regiment, and that's the person who would have been attending the collegium meetings instead of the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all I wanted to know because your prior answer didn't say Chief of Staff of the regiment, so I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, 65 ter document 5807 shall be assigned Exhibit P2428. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 6122.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, let me just ask you with respect to the conclusions that were drawn or reached during this -- during this briefing, were you apprised of that when you returned to the command post in June of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: No, no. You have to try and understand the time and the situation. In my statement, I stated that I was not discharged from hospital. I left hospital of my own will. Because of the gravity of the situation on the front line, and I was thrown in at the deep end, there was no time for long briefings or debriefings or explanations as to what had happened from the 13th or the 12th of October, 1994 when I was wounded until the day when I returned. It was just brief information as to where the units were deployed, what the situation was. There was fierce fighting on the Sarajevo front line. We came under attack in Crna Rijeka. We didn't talk about that. We didn't discuss that. We just acted. There was no time for long briefings and stories as to what happened. There was no time. I'm not saying that there was no need. If the times had been different, more normal, then things would have been done by the book and the commander would have been appraised of the most important things that had happened during his absence from the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you. I appreciate that. What I'm showing you here, as you can see from the title, is the schedule of this combat readiness briefing. And if we go to the second page. I think we have to be on the same page in the B/C/S. Page 1. All right. And we can see here at this briefing what essentially was in the order: At 1150 to 1210 hours that the problems of security or intelligence in 1994 will be addressed by General Tolimir. And basically conclusion based on the elevation of the situation, the battle-field, and the strategic evaluation of the future course of the war. Now, with respect to this document, if we go to 1900 hours, it's on page 4 in the English and it will be probably be page 2 -- I'm sorry, page 3 in the B/C/S. Just the page before this, I think. Yeah. At 1900 hours we see that. It says: "Discussion by other guests from the state leadership, RS state organs." I take it you've been to one of these kinds of briefings before yourself. Is that -- is that fair? Or accurate?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: Yes. In view of the nature of my job and things that happened at -- I attended just one collegium in January 1996, after the end of the war, but there is nothing in dispute here. This was the established method of briefing per combat readiness elements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'd like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours 65 ter document 6122 shall be assigned Exhibit P2429. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'd like to show the witness 65 ter 5837.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And while that's coming up, let me just ask you: Would your unit be involved in securing the facilities where such a briefing would be held?

utterances.speaker: MILOMIR SAVCIC
utterances.text: That's -- that was one of the key tasks of the military police battalion, in terms of security. And that was protection or providing security for facilities, institutions, military personnel sectors, axes, and so on and so forth. That was one of the key tasks of the military police, to provide security. And if such activities took place at the command place of the Main Staff or a rear command post, then it was the battalion of the military police that provided security.
